content: The greatest discomfort and pain were reported between three to six hours after the placement of the device, primarily due to ischemia caused by the device. Most participants in the studies were provided with analgesics, such as paracetamol and ibuprofen, to manage pain at home as needed. These medications were effective in controlling pain during the early ischemic phase for a significant proportion of clients. Pain experienced while wearing the device was reported to be less severe compared to similar time points following conventional surgery, even during erections. Participants reported transient but intense pain during device removal, as necrotic tissue was removed and the elastic and inner rings were detached from the healing wound. Approximately 43% of clients reported a Visual Analog Scale (VAS) pain score of 4 or higher during this process. Procedure times for device placement and removal varied significantly across studies, with more experienced providers achieving shorter procedure times. Cosmetic outcomes, considered an important measure of success, were reported under the values and preferences section. The quality of evidence supporting the recommendations was rated as moderate, and the strength of the recommendation was conditional in favor of the intervention. Devices prequalified through the WHO program may include multiple devices with different mechanisms of action, each with unique characteristics that must be considered during selection and use. WHO prequalification decisions are time-limited, and products and manufacturing sites on the WHO list of prequalified male circumcision devices are reassessed regularly. A recommendation for device use in younger male adolescents (under 18 years) will be considered when additional data become available. The strength of the recommendation was based on the quality of evidence, the balance of anticipated benefits and harms, client and healthcare provider values and preferences, and resource implications. A conditional recommendation was made due to concerns about potential harms, such as device slippage and displacement, in routine healthcare settings where evidence was insufficient. Uncertainty regarding patient acceptability and program costs also warranted a conditional recommendation. WHO prequalified male circumcision devices are considered efficacious, safe, and acceptable as additional methods for male circumcision to prevent HIV among healthy men aged 18 years and older in high HIV prevalence, resource-limited settings. This recommendation applies in settings where healthcare providers, including physicians and mid-level providers, are appropriately trained and competent in using the specific device, and where surgical backup facilities and skills are available as needed. The evidence profile tables in Annex 2 (available on the WHO website) provide a detailed quality assessment for each outcome. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was rated separately, while observational studies supplemented and validated the evidence from comparative trials. Only critical outcomes were considered when determining the overall quality of evidence. Although the evidence applies only to men aged 18 years or older, the overall quality of evidence was not downgraded for indirectness; instead, the recommendation was restricted to this age group. The overall quality of evidence for critical outcomes was rated as moderate, the lowest rating among critical outcomes. The judgment of the methodologists and the WHO secretariat was that further research would be unlikely to change the estimates of effect for eligibility, successful circumcision, and serious or moderate adverse events (AEs), especially if evidence from RCTs is supplemented by observational studies. For healing times, it was judged that while further data might change the magnitude of the difference between devices and surgery, the main conclusion—that healing times were longer following device circumcision—would likely remain unchanged. A smaller proportion of men were eligible for circumcision with a device (93–98%) compared to surgery. Men ineligible for the device method would require conventional surgical circumcision to obtain the HIV prevention benefits of circumcision. Unsuccessful device circumcisions were due to insufficient removal of the foreskin or the need to complete the procedure using a conventional surgical method. Healing times for devices were one to two weeks longer than for surgical circumcision. There is a theoretical higher risk of HIV acquisition with unprotected sex before the wound is healed. However, modeling suggests that any increased risk during the six-week healing period is negligible compared to the reduced lifetime risk of HIV acquisition after the wound is healed. The extension of the healing period by an additional one or two weeks also has negligible additional impact. When performed by appropriately trained healthcare providers in adequately resourced settings, the frequency of adverse events with devices was no higher than with conventional surgery. Most adverse events associated with device use were mild or moderate. A few events, including device displacements and slippage, required immediate or urgent surgical intervention to prevent potentially serious long-term outcomes. All three landmark randomized trials on the effect of male circumcision (MC) on heterosexual HIV acquisition assessed adverse events associated with surgical MC. These studies consistently found low rates of adverse events within the study environment. However, it is not possible to directly compare the occurrence of adverse events across different studies. Pain levels reported with devices were similar to or lower than those reported after conventional surgery. Device-based procedures took less than half the time required for conventional surgical procedures, including both placement and removal times. Overall, men reported high levels of satisfaction with the cosmetic results of their circumcised penises, regardless of whether a device or conventional surgery was used. However, the quality of data on cosmetic results was considered low due to indirectness and the risk of bias, as neither patients nor observers were blinded. For the elastic collar compression device, satisfaction with cosmetic results at six weeks or 90 days (depending on the study) was similarly high for both groups. For the collar clamp device, significantly more men in the device group reported being very satisfied compared to the surgery group. Devices may leave a more standardized circular wound appearance than conventional surgical methods at two weeks, six weeks, 60, or 90 days post-procedure, and they leave no suture marks. However, long-term data on cosmetic outcomes, such as at one year post-procedure, were unavailable for any method. The impact of the presence and appearance of necrotic tissue associated with the elastic collar compression device on acceptability has not been directly studied and remains unknown. Odor was reported in some studies on the elastic collar compression device. At times, the client’s partner or friends noticed the odor during the week the device was in place, and healthcare providers noticed it during device removal. Healing takes one to two weeks longer following device placement than with surgical methods. Therefore, men undergoing MC with a device must be counseled to abstain from sexual activity for a longer period than those undergoing conventional surgical MC, or a total of seven weeks on average. During the first week, while wearing the device, abstinence from all sexual activity is essential to prevent device displacement and potentially serious complications. Abstinence after device removal is essential until the wound is healed, which takes an average of six more weeks but can be as long as 8–9 weeks in some men. If sex is resumed before the wound is healed, condom use is essential to protect the healing wound and prevent HIV transmission. A study in Zambia reported that 24% of men in a routine surgical MC service setting acknowledged engaging in sexual activity before six weeks post-surgery. Of those, 46% had sex within the first three weeks, 82% reported at least one unprotected sex act, and 37% reported sex with two or more partners. While data on men’s resumption of sex after device-based circumcision were lacking, some men may find MC with a device unacceptable due to the slightly longer period of sexual abstinence. Several observational and comparative studies have reported on the effect of MC on clients’ work and daily activities. These studies consistently found that circumcision using devices minimally interfered with clients’ work or daily activities, except for sexual activity. Despite the consistency of findings, the overall quality of evidence regarding interference with daily activities was considered low due to indirectness and the risk of bias, as neither patients nor observers were blinded. Although both devices studied need to be worn for a week post-placement, their designs differ. For the collar clamp device, 28% of men in a small pilot study reported that the device disrupted sleep “somewhat” or “a lot,” 5% reported disruption of daily activities, and 10% reported disruption of work. In this study, 80% of men returned to work within two days after device placement. For the elastic collar compression device, greater interference with urination was reported compared to conventional surgery, but less interference with sleep, walking, working, and driving a motorbike was noted. Men undergoing device-based circumcision must return seven days later for safe device removal. While follow-up visits are usually advised after surgical MC, the sutures are absorbable and do not require removal, so some clients do not return. Evidence is lacking on whether the mandatory second visit for device removal influences acceptability. Return rates after surgical MC vary widely, with some studies reporting rates as low as 23% and others as high as 67%. Healthcare providers, including physicians and non-physicians, reported that performing circumcision using a device was easy. Many providers expressed a preference for devices over surgical methods, citing reasons such as ease of use, shorter procedure times, better cosmetic results, fewer complications, elimination of suturing, less bleeding, and, in the case of the elastic collar compression device, no need for routine injectable anesthesia. The quality of evidence supporting these findings was considered moderate to high. A systematic search of the literature identified studies on resource use and costs associated with MC. These studies were conducted in Zambia, Uganda, Kenya, and Zimbabwe. One study compared the collar clamp device to surgical circumcision.
